title: The Fall of the USSR, Pt II
summary: Part two of the Fall of the USSR. The hosts pick up after the December 1991 dissolution, covering the August 1991 coup against Gorbachev and Yeltsin's rise on a tank, Gorbachev's resignation, the West's limited economic response, Yeltsin's shock therapy reforms, the loans-for-shares privatization and rise of the Russian oligarchs, the social collapse of the 1990s (poverty, unemployment, alcoholism, falling life expectancy), Yeltsin's drinking and the 1993 parliament shelling, the 1992 televised Communist Party trial, and Putin's rise to power and consolidation of control over the oligarchs. Closes with a listener mail about Cornwall as a Celtic nation.

segments.title: Opening banter and part two setup
segments.summary: Hosts open the episode, joke about the intro and fashion, and set up part two of the Fall of the Soviet Union.
topics: Fall of the USSR part two

segments.title: Dissolution and the August coup
segments.summary: The USSR was dissolved in December 1991 and Russia's future was uncertain. The hosts describe the failed hardliner coup against Gorbachev, during which Yeltsin addressed crowds from a tank, and how the coup ended up weakening Gorbachev.

segments.title: Gorbachev's resignation and Russia's new status
segments.summary: Gorbachev peacefully handed over power after the coup, and the Soviet presidency was abolished. Russia became the Russian Federation, and the hosts discuss the end of Soviet superpower status.

segments.title: Loss of Soviet identity and Western response
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how the loss of Soviet identity left many citizens unmoored, including Putin's reported reaction. They note the West, under George H. W. Bush, offered limited help to rebuild Russia.
topics: George H. W. Bush Russia policy

segments.title: Goodbye Lenin reference and US aid stance
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how Western help focused on Russia's economy rather than friendship, and mention the German film Goodbye Lenin suggested by a listener.

segments.title: Shock therapy and economic reforms
segments.summary: Yeltsin and economist Yegor Gaidar pursued shock therapy, a rapid move to a free market. Reforms included making the ruble convertible and removing state price controls.

segments.title: Privatization and voucher program
segments.summary: The government distributed vouchers for shares in state-owned enterprises to most citizens. Many Russians believed the shock therapy was deliberately inflicted by the West.

segments.title: Hyperinflation and rise of oligarchs via vouchers
segments.summary: Hyperinflation devalued savings, and people traded vouchers for goods. Vouchers were concentrated into a few hands, creating the Russian oligarchs.

segments.title: Loans for shares and asset stripping
segments.summary: In 1996 the government loaned shares in major state firms to oligarchs for quick cash, and those firms were later sold. Putin was among those who gained a controlling stake in a nickel company. Oligarchs stripped raw materials for export, causing factory closures and unemployment.

segments.title: Social collapse of the 1990s
segments.summary: Poverty rose sharply, the Soviet safety net disappeared, the birth rate fell, and heavy drinking contributed to a steep drop in male life expectancy.

segments.title: Shock therapy's political fallout and elite continuity
segments.summary: The hosts compare the post-Soviet backlash to Versailles and Hitler's rise. Elites from the Soviet nomenclatura kept their power after communism's fall.

segments.title: Yeltsin's drinking and the 1993 crisis
segments.summary: Yeltsin's public antics and heavy drinking are described, including a state visit conducting a parade band and a reported late-night taxi incident in Washington. In 1993 parliament impeached him, he dissolved it, and military forces shelled the parliament building, while Western governments largely viewed him favorably. His approval fell to very low levels.

segments.title: 1996 election and Yeltsin's grip on power
segments.summary: The 1996 privatization scheme is described as designed to keep Yeltsin in power against an expected Communist victory. The hosts note Russians felt cheated by Gorbachev and then Yeltsin.

segments.title: Communist Party trial and lustration
segments.summary: Yeltsin banned the Communist Party, and a 1992 televised trial put Soviet communism on trial without individual defendants. The KGB had been renamed the FSB, and a lustration proposal was made, with its proposer assassinated in 1998. Yeltsin's symbolic moves, like changing the anthem and flag, were divisive.

segments.title: Putin's rise and consolidation of power
segments.summary: Putin was appointed prime minister, pounded Chechnya, and became president in 1999 as Yeltsin left office. He brought the oligarchs under control, jailed Khodorkovsky, and the economy recovered on oil exports.

segments.title: Wrap-up of part two
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the two-part episode and transition to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail on Cornwall
segments.summary: A listener notes that Cornwall is a Celtic nation with its own language and was recognized as a national minority by the UK, correcting the earlier UK episode. The hosts thank him.
